metadata.title: PISA Computer-Based Assessment of Student Skills in Science (EN)

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The analysis uses PISA 2006 CBAS main-study data for Denmark, Iceland, and Korea, with sampling designed to be representative at the country level. To account for selection biases in schools and students, the PISA data are weighted using a balanced repeated replication (BRR) method, which adjusts for over- or under-representation of geographical areas within countries. Statistical significance testing and standard errors are computed using the PISA replicate-weight procedures (80 replicate weights on plausible values). The report does not name a single weight variable (e.g., W_FSTUWT), but it explicitly states that BRR replicate weights were used for inference on plausible-value-based achievement scores.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The report describes that CBAS achievement scores were generated using plausible values and that replicate weights were used for significance testing, but it does not provide a specific missing-data handling rule for student-level questionnaire or background variables used in any models. Missing responses to CBAS items are reported as very low (<1%), and some CBAS items were dropped/combined prior to analysis, but the paper does not state whether missing questionnaire/background data were imputed, deleted, or otherwise handled. This is therefore a reporting gap for missing-data handling at the analytic-variable level.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The report focuses on the PISA 2006 computer-based assessment of scientific literacy (CBAS) administered in the main study in three countries: Denmark, Iceland, and Korea. It includes (i) all students who participated in the CBAS test session and (ii) all PISA-participating students from CBAS-participating schools in Iceland, Denmark, and Korea. For Iceland, the original CBAS sample had 1,104 students with a 71% CBAS response rate; the CBAS analyses additionally impute CBAS plausible values for 2,782 students who attended CBAS-participating schools but did not respond to CBAS, yielding 3,566 students in the CBAS analyses. In Denmark and Korea, the final data file includes all students participating in CBAS or PISA from the sampled CBAS schools, with reported CBAS-responding counts used for the achievement comparisons.

data.outcome_summary: This OECD report compares PISA 2006 science achievement delivered via computer-based assessment of scientific literacy (CBAS) versus the standard paper-and-pencil science test in three countries (Denmark, Iceland, Korea). The CBAS main study used a fixed-form computer test with 45 multimedia-extended items (final analyses on 42 items after dropping/combining specific items), administered on standardized laptops with two item orders split to reduce fatigue. Achievement scores were scaled on a PISA-like metric and re-standardised for comparability within the report; CBAS and paper scores were based on plausible values, and inference used PISA’s balanced repeated replication (BRR) with replicate weights. At the country level, overall performance did not change by modality, but gender differences did: males outperformed females on CBAS in all three countries, while gender patterns differed on paper. The report also documents that CBAS was less confounded by reading ability (weaker association with reading than in paper-based science) and that students reported higher enjoyment/motivation for CBAS, yet these engagement measures showed weak or non-existent associations with achievement on CBAS.
data.null_fields_interpretation: This is an OECD technical report chapter summarizing comparative assessment results rather than an empirical machine-learning study that trains predictive models. Consequently, there are no ML algorithms, ML target variables, or model performance metrics to extract into the main_findings table. The report does, however, provide detailed assessment design, sampling/weighting logic, and modality-by-gender achievement comparisons using PISA plausible-value scaling and BRR replicate-weight inference.
